result:
**The proposed answer q^{2h} is wrong.** I checked it in the simplest case, h = 1.

For h = 1, the (h−1)-spaces are points, so X is a set of points in PG(3,q) with at most t points on any plane. The claimed bound is |X| = (t−2)q + t.

**Testing t = q^{2h} = q² at h = 1.** The bound gives N = q³ + q² − 2q. Count incidences between points and planes. Each point lies on q²+q+1 planes, and PG(3,q) has q³+q²+q+1 planes, so the average number of points of X per plane is

N(q²+q+1) / (q³+q²+q+1).

Multiplying out, N(q²+q+1) = q⁵ + 2q⁴ − q² − 2q, while q²(q³+q²+q+1) = q⁵ + q⁴ + q³ + q². The first exceeds the second for q ≥ 2, so the average exceeds q². Some plane would then contain more than q² points, contradicting t = q². So t = q² is impossible here.

**A value that does fit.** Take t = q+1 at h = 1. The bound gives (q−1)q + q + 1 = q² + 1, which is exactly the size of an ovoid of PG(3,q). An ovoid meets every plane in 1 or q+1 points, and ovoids exist for all q. This suggests the general answer is t = q^h + 1, which gives |X| = q^{2h} + 1, the natural q-analogue of an ovoid. This generalisation is my inference from the h = 1 case and the pattern, not a result I verified.

The proposed solution also relies on an unsupported "general pattern" q^{(k−2)h} and on a claimed k = 3 result that I did not verify.

VERDICT: REJECT
